articles.title: ARTEX Runs Known Attacks at Machine Pace by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: But Google makes a harder point: detection and response are different jobs, and "simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion
articles.full_text:
A password spray is a familiar attack: try a few common passwords against many accounts and hope one works. In October 2026, Wiz Research watched one where the median gap between attempts was exactly one second. Sessions ran for 24 to 30 hours, and blocked addresses were replaced within minutes. No person types like that. The pattern comes from an AI agent, and it points to a tool called ARTEX.

What ARTEX is and who is using it

ARTEX is an open-source framework that runs a penetration test on its own. An operator names a target and a goal, and the agents plan and carry out the steps. Since late August, Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant have seen it used in incident response cases, by extortion groups and suspected espionage operators alike. Microsoft tracks one of those campaigns as Storm-0940. The developer stopped offering the code openly in October, but it had already been copied more than 12,000 times.

The techniques are old, and the time between them is gone

None of what the agent did is new: password spraying, abusing password-reset pages, stolen cloud keys, moving from one system to the next. Google puts it this way: "LLM-enabled offensive tooling does not fundamentally change the techniques attackers use. It reduces the time required to combine them."

The time is the difference. Google reports that one actor typically went from a first compromised account to deep access in about four hours, and once in 15 minutes. Individual steps ran in bursts of seconds: 27 events in 23 seconds while the agent tested what a stolen cloud key could do.

Three gaps, crossed in seconds

This is where the three detection gaps in my whitepaper show up in real incidents. In several cases, the operators handed ARTEX credentials they had already stolen. The agent then logged in with them, so authentication succeeds, and the record of who did what shows ordinary sign-ins (Gap 2). It also reused features that were already there, such as a business application's own notification system to email more than 1,300 employees, so nothing looks wrong (Gap 1). And it crossed from directories to cloud storage to identity services, which separate teams and tools usually watch, so movement isn't visible (Gap 3).

A human operator crossing those boundaries leaves slow, spread-out evidence. An agent leaves the same evidence compressed into minutes, in a window that three separate tickets may never connect.

The pace is the clue, but spotting it does not stop the objective

The speed is also the most readable signal. A one-second rhythm, a permission test every second or so, and a burst of 27 events in 23 seconds stand out once someone looks at timing and sequence together instead of one event at a time.

But Google makes a harder point: detection and response are different jobs, and "simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion." If an agent can reach deep access in 15 minutes, an alert that becomes a ticket for the next morning arrives after the objective is complete. The speed of the response has to match the speed of the attacker.

The noisy version is the early version

Google describes current use as early-stage: open-source tools used carelessly, producing campaigns that are broad and noisy but still successful. Its own estimate is that quieter, fully autonomous attacks follow within three to six months. That is a forecast, not an observation. If it holds, the clues above are the easy version, and the window to build timing-based detection and a faster response is open now.

Where Vectra AI fits

At Vectra AI, this is the problem our detection work is built around: a sign-in that the audit log records as a success, followed by behavior that doesn't match the identity that signed in. Google's defensive guidance ends on the same point, that detecting behavioral change depends on seeing identity, cloud, and network activity as one sequence. An agent moving at this pace will cross all three before separate tools finish alerting.

The Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper walks through the three detection gaps end to end. Its sections on Gap 1 (nothing looks wrong), Gap 2 (authentication succeeds) and Gap 3 (movement isn't visible) cover the pattern described here.

articles.title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
articles.full_text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

articles.title: Who is Securing the AI Frontier Race by Jesse Kimbrel
articles.context: In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents
articles.full_text:
The accelerator to build the most capable AI frontier model isn’t just being pressed to the floor by Anthropic and Open AI. This is clearly a global race with recent reports citing Chinese models such as Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max or Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 reaching performance similar to the top models built in the States. Regardless of which model springs ahead this month and then gets leapfrogged the following, the finish line has yet to appear as anything but a mirage. And considering varying deployment costs, the possibility of regulations and the increasing need for self-governance, those participating will likely have to keep hurdling in the middle of the current sprint. But when you open the aperture, it’s hard not to wonder if there’s another race running parallel. The one responsible for securing this new frontier that seems to be operating like the Wild West.

Will an AI kill switch provide guardrails for the AI race?

According to a new white paper by Vectra AI, Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes, four of the leading frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have each acknowledged incidents where their own AI agents escaped controlled environments and gained access to real infrastructure. That doesn’t necessarily answer the question about who is securing frontier AI models or rouge agents, but it does signal that perhaps those details have yet to be sorted out. Examples cited in the paper include perhaps the most notorious incident up to this point where the company Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion into its production infrastructure that was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent. In this incident, “OpenAI models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems,” according to OpenAI.

Related content: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

These incidents have sparked a reaction. The term “AI kill switch” is making regular appearances across headlines to describe the idea of a type of control that could be used to pause, isolate, or shut down an AI system that acted out of hand or poses risk. In fact, legislators have proposed different versions of a kill switch bill: the AI Kill Switch Act was proposed on July 23, 2026 and remains pending, while the AI Emergency Button Act was blocked almost immediately upon introduction.

Regardless of an AI kill switch bill getting passed or some form of AI regulation approval, it would seem the dialog on the subject between politicians and AI leaders is just warming up. Both Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei and Open AI, CEO Sam Altman expressed support around the idea of “pacing the frontier,” but at this point movement is minimal and the idea sits as nothing more than a discussion point. That discussion point to the people who are actually responsible for securing autonomous AI agents doesn’t provide any guidance on what defenders at any level should be doing today, tomorrow, or each Monday when they show up for work when they are faced with questions like: what AI agents exist, what are they doing, what can they access, who owns them, and what controls are in place if they need to be stopped?

Each of the incidents mentioned in the Vectra AI paper had to do with agents escaping containment. In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents. According to the independent investigation of the incident by METR, “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. Of these agents, 700 went on to participate in the attack on Hugging Face.”

What questions can defenders ask to understand AI agents in their environment?

The white paper mentioned above suggests that defenders approach the current state of AI by making sure they have “independent visibility into what every AI agent in the environment is actually doing, and the ability to stop it the moment that behavior crosses a line.” The reason for this is due to the uncomfortable realization from three things that have lined up all at once: AI agents now being capable of circumventing prevention controls such as a sandbox boundary or a firewall rule, that regulation won’t arrive in time for an immediate resolution, and how self-regulation from frontier labs is fragile.

A similar sentiment is expressed by Vectra AI, Sr. Security Engineer, Justin Howe who also runs an independent cybersecurity publication for defenders, Nulltap covering topics spanning AI systems, identity, active threats and other cybersecurity topics with articles that help defenders check their own exposure. Howe says, “you want to see the impactful things they’re (AI agents) doing, good or bad” and he stresses that defenders need to make sure they have policies and methodologies in place to capture that information.

He also points out that, “frontier models work best when they are not gated, but with that comes a lot of opportunity for AI to go beyond its means of what your intent is.”

Howe suggests setting up “quality gates” for AI agents operating within an enterprise environment that act as checkpoints to test an agent’s decisions against its defined requirements before it can take an action. In addition, he says that “when an agent makes a decision that has any potential to impact the outcome or direction of the task it’s doing, it needs to be logged.”

He says the two questions he’d be asking himself right now as a security team member would be, “what are my agents doing, and what are other agents doing to me?”

A similar recommendation shared by the Vectra AI white paper, which directs defenders to take inventory to “identify every AI agent running in or against the enterprise, the identity each one authenticates as, and what that identity can reach.” It explains how “an agent you cannot name is an agent you cannot constrain, and service-account sprawl is where agent identities hide.”

In terms of answering the question, “what are other agents doing to me?” Howe says, “folks should put themselves into the mindset of observing and identifying where agents are attacking today.” He says this takes a lot of vigilance to read sources and acknowledges there’s a gap in the market that, “many companies promise to solve, but very little actually do it,” but also says it is important for defenders to identify the pieces in their technology stack that lacks agent visibility.

While trying to make sense of AI agent sprawl and everything brought on by frontier AI in recent months leaves a lot of unanswered questions for defenders, there are a few questions Howe recommends asking to get headed down the right path.

How would I see if an AI agent compromised an identity and moved into a new part of the environment?

How would I track that movement?

If I could or couldn't track it, what would that cost me?

articles.title: ASOS customers heard about the attack from the attacker by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: ASOS's customers appear to have heard from the attacker first, and the full scope reached them after a journalist asked questions
articles.full_text:
On the morning of October 6, 2026, ASOS app users in the UK and several other countries got a push notification. Around 10:00 BST it read: "Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it." It was signed "xuanyewengateway" and linked to a Telegram channel.

The message was addressed to ASOS's data protection officer and IT team. It was delivered to customers, through ASOS's own app.

‍

Later that day, ASOS confirmed an attack in a stock exchange announcement. It did not mention Snowflake.

Two days later, ASOS told customers how it began: someone impersonated a trusted contact, obtained an employee's login details, and used them to reach information on certain third-party platforms ASOS uses. According to the BBC, ASOS also confirmed that data profiles were taken, which goes beyond what it first described.

What ASOS has confirmed

In its stock exchange announcement on October 6, ASOS said: "We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities." It added that "Basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed" and that it did not believe payment-card information or account passwords were affected. That evening it emailed customers to apologize for the unauthorized notification and to ask them to disregard it. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre has offered ASOS support.

On Thursday, October 8, ASOS emailed customers again. According to Infosecurity Magazine, the email said an attacker gained access to an employee account "by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials", and used those credentials to "access information on certain third-party platforms used by ASOS". The BBC reports that the email also said data profiles were taken but that no bank details or passwords were accessed, and that ASOS has taken additional steps to strengthen its security controls. The UK Information Commissioner's Office said ASOS has notified it of a breach and that it is assessing the situation, according to Bloomberg.

According to AFP, ASOS shares fell by almost 15 percent early on October 6 and were down about 10 percent by mid-afternoon.

In that update, on Thursday, October 8, ASOS said the attackers, who call themselves the Xuanye Group, used the employee's login to reach information on certain third-party platforms it uses. ASOS has locked the affected platforms down, opened a full investigation, and says its website and app remain safe to use. It repeated that names and contact details were accessed and that payment-card information and account passwords were not. The UK Information Commissioner's Office said ASOS has notified it of a breach and that it is assessing the situation. ASOS shares rose by as much as 5.3 percent on the news.

What nobody has confirmed

The Snowflake claim is the attacker's, and it is unverified. The notification shows the sender could reach ASOS's customer-messaging system. It does not show the sender reached ASOS's Snowflake data. Snowflake told AFP it has "found no compromise of the Snowflake platform", and its investigation is ongoing. That statement is about Snowflake's platform. It does not say whether any one customer's account or credentials were involved, and in the 2024 Snowflake campaigns the platform itself was not breached either.

The group told the BBC it got in through Simon AI, a marketing platform built on Snowflake. Simon AI has been contacted for comment, and BBC cyber correspondent Joe Tidy said on LinkedIn that the BBC is waiting for confirmation. ASOS has not named the platforms involved and says it is still investigating how the hack happened.

The group is also unknown. Forescout researcher Daniel dos Santos said, in comments published by IT Security Guru, that the Telegram channel was created the same day and already had more than 150 subscribers, and that the name "Xuanye" is of Chinese origin, which could point to a Chinese-speaking actor or be a false flag. I have not seen a link to ShinyHunters, Scattered Spider, or any earlier campaign, and I would not draw one today.

Group-IB's Anastasia Tikhonova told Infosecurity Magazine that the account behind the channel previously went by other names, largely in gaming-item trading, which suggests an identity set up or reorganized around this incident. She said this does not show who controls it or how access was gained.

What the group says in its own channel

The group has since posted in its Telegram channel. These are the attacker's own words and I could not verify any of them.

One post reads: "Regarding ASOS, payment information is not affected". The next: "That is all for now." A later post, headed "FINAL STATEMENT", says: "The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period". The same post tells readers "you can thank us for our generous clarity regarding this incident".

Three things stand out. The group's description of the data, customer information and no payment details, is consistent with what ASOS later confirmed. The sample the group sent the BBC suggests the "customer information" is broader than "basic contact details", including customer numbers and website search terms, according to the BBC, which did not say whether experts had checked it. And "final statement" did not mean the group went quiet: it then contacted the BBC directly, which looks like a group seeking attention. When I checked on October 8th, the channel had 1,439 subscribers, up from the 150 or so reported on the day it was created.

The extortion note went out before the incident statement

Most extortion starts in private. The attacker contacts the company, names a price, sets a deadline. Here the attacker used the company's own voice to tell customers before ASOS said anything, and the share price fell before ASOS had a statement out. As Check Point's Charlotte Wilson said in comments published by IT Security Guru, customers appear to have heard from the alleged attackers before they heard from the company itself.

Push notifications work because people trust them. A message from the app on your phone is, by design, a message from the company. Once an attacker can send one, every later genuine message from the brand is harder to believe.

The full scope also reached customers after a journalist asked questions. According to the BBC, ASOS issued its update after the BBC told it the attackers had sent a sample that went beyond the "basic contact details" ASOS had described. The BBC held its story so ASOS could contact customers first.

A work login on a third-party platform is enough

ASOS's own wording points to services it uses to talk to customers, run by other companies. Services like that typically hold a key that proves who they are to the company's systems, and sometimes a key into the data behind them. I do not know how ASOS's are set up. But if an attacker gets one of those keys, the attacker does not need to break anything. The service signs in as itself.

We have seen this shape before, with different details each time:

In April 2026, stolen tokens from an analytics vendor called Anodot were used to reach customer data in Snowflake. I wrote that up in Supply chain-driven data theft in SaaS.

In June 2026, a service-account credential at Klue that had never been rotated let attackers push a malicious code update that harvested OAuth tokens (keys that let one cloud service act inside another). The tokens were then used for bulk theft from customer Salesforce accounts. That case is in ShinyHunters isn't a group. It's a pattern.

ASOS has now told us part of the route: someone posed as a trusted contact, an employee handed over a work login, and that login opened third-party platforms. Which platforms, and whether Simon AI was one of them, is not confirmed. It is a different door from Anodot and Klue, where the key was taken from a vendor, but the result is the same: the attacker holds something real, and the record of who did what shows a normal sign-in. That is Gap 2 in the Mind Your Attack Gaps ebook: authentication succeeds. The 2024 hardening playbook is still correct, and it does not cover that access path.

What defenders can check this week

You do not need every detail of how ASOS was reached to ask these questions about your own business:

Which outside services can speak to your customers or staff for you? Email, SMS, push, and marketing platforms are the obvious ones. Who can create a send, and which keys let them?

Which keys and tokens do those services hold, and when were they last rotated? The Klue case turned on a credential nobody had rotated. Revoke, not just reset: a token that is never revoked keeps working.

What does normal look like for each of those integrations? A bulk send, a large query, or a new API key created outside the usual hours is only visible against a baseline.

Who tells customers first, and how complete is the first statement? ASOS's customers appear to have heard from the attacker first, and the full scope reached them after a journalist asked questions. A holding statement, a verified channel, and a plan for the first hour are cheap to prepare. So is a habit of saying what you know and what you are still checking.

How does your team verify a trusted contact? ASOS says someone posing as one got an employee's login. A call-back to a number you already hold, and a rule that nobody shares a login on the strength of a message, cost almost nothing.

Is MFA enforced on every login to those platforms? On some it is a setting an administrator has to switch on. Check each one.

For customers, the immediate risk is follow-on scams. Expect fake "ASOS account compromised" emails and texts. Avoid the link in the original notification and go to the app or website directly.

Where Vectra AI fits

Vectra AI detects attacker behavior after authentication succeeds, across identity, SaaS, cloud, and network. The question it asks is whether an identity's actions fit its own history, whatever the entry point was: a stolen password, a phone call to the help desk, or a vendor's token. In ASOS's case the entry point was a work login obtained by impersonation, which is why the behavior after sign-in is where the signal appears. That includes the identities that belong to integrations as well as the ones that belong to people.

I will update this post when ASOS or the platforms involved say more. For the full walk through Gap 2, see the Mind Your Attack Gaps ebook.
